narrative:
The model estimates a 57% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key aspects of your profile that, according to patterns seen across many similar employees, point toward a higher likelihood of departure.

The strongest factor is the number of training programs you attended in the last three years. While most employees who stay complete far fewer or none at all, you have participated in seven or more. Surprisingly, this high level of training actually pushes the model toward predicting you will leave, possibly because it signals you are actively building skills that could lead you elsewhere.

Next, your overall years of experience (6–10 years) and your tenure in your current role (1–5 years) both work against you. Compared with employees the model expects to stay—who are more often in the 1–5 years overall experience bracket—your mid-level experience appears to give you more external options, nudging the prediction toward leaving.

Taken together, these elements outweigh other positive signals such as your satisfaction with rewards, recognition, and work-life balance. The organization should discuss your career goals with you openly and explore whether additional responsibilities, clearer advancement paths, or further tailored development could increase your commitment and reduce the risk of departure.
